transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm here because occupational health at the department sent me. They're saying I'm not eating enough to be on duty. But honestly, I just stick to a routine. Most days I'll have black coffee, maybe a plain yogurt, and then just a few bites of chicken at night. If I eat a full meal, it just feels like... like I'm letting my standards slip, you know? I need to stay sharp.
When you think about eating more, are you mainly worried about gaining weight or changing your body shape, or is it more about keeping your daily routine strict and disciplined regardless of weight?

It's the weight. The discipline is part of it, but... if I step on the scale and it's up even half a pound, I get this jolt. It's like I've completely lost control. When that happens, I'll spend the rest of the day cutting back even harder. I just really can't stand the idea of putting weight back on.
Can you tell me your current height and weight, and how that compares to what's typical or healthy for you?

Well, the nurse at occupational health checked my vitals before sending me here. She told me my weight was dangerously low for my height. I mean, I can see that my uniform hangs off me now. I've actually had to tighten my duty belt way past the old notches just to keep it secure. But honestly... when she told me it was dangerously low, I still just thought to myself that I could stand to be a little sharper. It really doesn't feel like a problem to me.

latest_inference.note: Confirmed significantly low body weight (dangerously low per exam), intense fear of weight gain, and denial/minimization of severity - meeting full criteria for anorexia nervosa rather than atypical presentation, ruling out F50.1.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with significantly low body weight (confirmed by occupational health nurse as 'dangerously low' for height, uniform hanging loose, belt tightened past prior notches), an intense fear of weight gain (jolt/loss of control reaction to half-pound increase), persistent behavior to prevent weight gain (severe caloric restriction to black coffee, plain yogurt, and minimal chicken), and a distorted perception/minimization of the seriousness of the low body weight ('doesn't feel like a problem to me' despite medical concern). These features meet criteria for Anorexia Nervosa, restricting type (F50.0), rather than binge-purge subtype (F50.2) or atypical presentation (F50.1), as there is no mention of binge eating or purging behaviors, and the weight loss/restriction is severe and clearly driven by fear of weight gain rather than general body image concerns alone.

confirmed_symptoms: Severe caloric restriction (black coffee, plain yogurt, few bites of chicken daily)
Avoidance of full meals due to perceived loss of discipline
Intense distress ('jolt') upon minor weight increase (half a pound)
Compensatory further restriction after perceived weight gain
Explicit statement of inability to tolerate weight regain
Minimization of medically confirmed dangerously low weight
Belief that being thinner equates to being 'sharper' or more disciplined
Lack of insight into severity despite visible physical changes (loose uniform, tightened belt)
Nurse-confirmed dangerously low weight for height
Visible physical wasting (uniform hangs off patient, belt tightened past prior notches)

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Not explicitly quantified in months, but pattern described as an established daily routine ('most days') suggesting a persistent, ongoing pattern rather than acute onset.
additional_requirements: Low body weight confirmed by objective medical assessment (occupational health nurse)
Fear of weight gain confirmed as primary driver over general discipline/routine concerns
Denial/minimization of medical seriousness of low weight confirmed
No binge eating or purging behaviors reported, supporting restricting subtype
